title: Angioedema | NHS inform
text:
Angioedema
Angioedema is swelling of the deeper layers of the skin. It’s caused by a build-up of fluid.
A man with light brown skin has a swollen lower lip. The lower lip is around the size of an adult thumb nail. The top lip is around half this size. The swollen lip is slightly red towards the inside of the mouth but the rest of the lips are a normal pink colour. The image is a close up view of this.
A man with white skin has a swollen right eye lid. The man has his eyes open but the upper right eye lid is swollen to the size of an adult finger nail. There is a little pinkness on and around the swollen eyelid.
Symptoms of angioedema
The main symptom of angioedema is swelling. This can affect any part of the body, including the:
face – particularly the lips, tongue and eyelids
hands or feet
genitals
The swollen area may be hot or painful.
If an allergic reaction has caused the swelling, you may also have a raised, itchy rash (
hives
).
Sometimes the bowel may become swollen which can cause stomach pain.
In severe cases, your throat may swell which can lead to breathing difficulties. This is a medical emergency and should be treated immediately.
Phone 999 if:
your lips, mouth, throat or tongue suddenly become swollen
you’re breathing very fast or struggling to breathe (you may become very wheezy or feel like you’re choking or gasping for air)
your throat feels tight or you’re struggling to swallow
your skin, tongue or lips turn blue, grey or pale (if you have black or brown skin, this may be easier to see on the palms of your hands or soles of your feet)
you suddenly become very confused, drowsy or dizzy
someone faints and can’t be woken up
a child is limp, floppy or not responding like they normally do (their head may fall to the side, backwards or forwards, or they may find it difficult to lift their head or focus on your face)
You or the person who’s unwell may also have a rash that’s swollen, raised or itchy.
These can be signs of a serious allergic reaction and may need immediate treatment in hospital.
Ask for an urgent GP appointment if:
part of your body suddenly becomes swollen (like your hands, feet or genitals)
Phone 111 if your GP practice is closed.
Diagnosing angioedema
Your healthcare professional will examine the swollen area and ask about your symptoms. This will help them to work out if you need any further tests.
Tell your doctor about any medications you’re taking, including over-the-counter medication. For example, painkillers, herbal supplements and vitamins.
You should not stop taking any prescribed medication unless you’re advised to by a healthcare professional.
Types of angioedema
There are different types of angioedema. These are:
acute allergic angioedema – an allergic reaction to certain foods, medicines or other substances
idiopathic angioedema – when there’s no obvious cause for angioedema
non-allergic angioedema – the swelling is a side effect of certain medications, most often angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors
hereditary angioedema – a rare type of angioedema that’s often inherited from your parents
acquired angioedema – a very rare type of angioedema that you can get if you have lymphoma (
cancer
) or
lupus
Treatment for angioedema
You may not need treatment for angioedema if it’s mild, or it only affects a small area of your body.
You’ll usually need emergency treatment in hospital if the swelling is:
severe
widespread
affects your lips, tongue or throat
Treatments for angioedema include:
antihistamines
and
corticosteroids
– to help reduce swelling
a different medication – if you’re taking one that seems to be causing your symptoms
steroid tablets – like prednisolone
If you have angioedema that keeps coming back (hereditary angioedema), you may also need medicine to stop this.
You may have regular reviews to check if your treatment is working.
If your symptoms do not improve or get worse, you may need to go back to hospital for further tests and treatment.
